notes.1a: This was answered well by most candidates. Weaker responses tended to include errors as a result of counting the electrons in the structures and ignoring the fact that some were ions.
notes.1b: Most candidates correctly identified F as the incorrect structure. Weaker responses had difficulty expressing the reason sufficiently well enough. The most common incorrect reasons given for choosing F were that ‘electrons are not paired in the outer shell’ or ‘the outer shell is not complete’. Cambridge International General Certificate of Secondary Education 0620 Chemistry November 2020
notes.1c: Candidates had to count the electrons (10) and realise that a 2 + charge meant that the number of protons exceeded the number of electrons by two. Many simply assumed number of electrons were equal to number of protons and gave 10 as their answer, whilst others assumed the number of protons was two less than the number of electrons.
notes.1di: This was found to be the most difficult part in the question. A species with two electrons and a charge of − 1 needs to contain 1 proton, thus H was the answer. Although ‘H’ was accepted, many incorrectly gave ‘hydrogen’.
notes.1dii: Most candidates realised that aluminium was the element whose ion had a 3 + charge and 10 electrons. Weaker responses opted for nitrogen, incorrectly.
notes.2a: Many candidates knew that the correct acid was nitric but wrote the name, which was not credited. ‘H 2 NO 3 ’ was a frequently seen error, as was ‘NO 3 ’. A significant number of candidates opted to make things hard for themselves by writing an equation for the reaction between nitric acid and a carbonate. If ‘HNO ’ was seen as a reactant, credit was given.
notes.2bi: The majority of candidates appreciated the need to react all the acid.
notes.2bii: Candidates need to be aware that observations are based upon what is seen rather than what can be concluded. Thus, ‘no more carbon dioxide given off’ received no credit as what would be seen is ‘no more effervescence’. Candidates who wrote ‘a precipitate forms’ received no credit for this response. Precipitates form when two solutions (react to) form a solid. Here, it was a solid not dissolving. Weaker responses described the reaction rather than its cessation, and phrases such as ‘fizzing’ and ‘dissolving’ were seen.
notes.2biii: Only the strongest of responses appreciated that (thoroughly) rinsing the residue would achieve a maximum yield of crystals.
notes.2biv: Although many candidates have learnt this description, a large number did not describe the key points of a saturated solution – ‘no more solute can dissolve’ and ‘at a stated temperature’. Weaker responses tended to confuse the terms solute and solvent or tended to describe saturation of organic molecules.
notes.2bv: A common incorrect answer was iron( II ) nitrate or the omission of the oxidation state when the oxide or hydroxide of iron was given. A large number of candidates gave oxides or hydroxides of metals other than iron, copper being a common example.
notes.2c: Better performing candidates were able to work their way through this structured calculation. The M of FeSO , wa s the mostly commonly seen. The mass of water, ‘152’, was often seen in working r 4 out but often did not feature on the answer line. The importance of candidates showing working should be stressed as those candidates who did so, often picked up marks as a result of ‘error carried forward’.
notes.2di: Very few candidates knew the term for making insoluble salts from solutions of two soluble salts was ‘precipitation’. ‘Filtration’ was frequently seen, presumably as a result of candidates focussing upon step 2 in the process.
notes.2dii: Better performing candidates were able to recall that AgBr forms a cream precipitate. Cambridge International General Certificate of Secondary Education 0620 Chemistry November 2020
notes.2diii: Candidates found this ionic equation for the formation of a binary insoluble compound difficult. It was evident that the idea of an ionic equation is not understood by many candidates. Many candidates opted to make things more difficult by giving a full equation. Others omitted ionic charges or state symbols.
notes.2e: Candidates need to be prepared to calculate answers by working with moles rather than reacting masses. Although there were many ways through this unstructured calculation, it was expected that candidates would determine the number of moles of NaC l being formed by dividing the mass formed by the M r of NaC l (2.34 ÷ 58.5) to give 0.04 mol. The next step is to consider the stoichiometry and to realise the number of mol of C l used was half that of NaC l formed (0.04 ÷ 2) to give 0.02. The third step was to convert the mol of C l 2 to its volume by multiplying by 24 000.
notes.2fi: It was expected that candidates would understand that conductivity of NaC l was based upon the fact it is ionically bonded and when solid, the ions are in fixed positions, whereas when molten, the ions are mobile. The best responses were succinct such as, ‘when solid, the ions in NaC l are in fixed positions and when molten, they can move’. ‘Free ions’ did not gain credit as it is not clear what they are free from. ‘Ions are free to move’, however, is creditworthy. Weaker responses confused electrons and ions and switched, after mentioning ions, to describe electron movement or lack of movement. Many candidates contradicted ‘ionic bonding’ as they introduced covalency into their response with phrases such as ‘NaC l has ionic bonding with strong inter-molecular forces’.
notes.2fii: Chlorine was well known as the product at the anode, although ‘chloride’ was commonly seen.
notes.2fiii: Candidates found this question about the redox process at an anode (‘electron loss’ and ‘oxidation’) during electrolysis challenging.
notes.2fiv: Nearly all candidates knew that aqueous conditions would also allow electrical conductivity.
notes.3a: This question required candidates to state two physical properties which are found in both Group I and transition elements. Most candidates were able to state either electrical conductivity, heat conductivity or malleability. A large number of candidates gave typical physical properties of most metals (such as high melting point, hardness and high density), which show a difference rather than similarity between these two types of metal. Other candidates gave more than two responses, a practice which should be discouraged if only two responses are asked for.
notes.3b: This question required candidates to state two physical properties which are different between each type of metal. Better responses focused upon the lower melting points and lower densities of Group I metals. A significant number of candidates wrote about chemical properties such as variable oxidation state and catalytic activity.
notes.3ci: Most candidates were able to name hydrogen as the gas evolved when sodium reacts with water.
notes.3cii: The identity of the ion responsible for alkalinity was known by most. Cambridge International General Certificate of Secondary Education 0620 Chemistry November 2020
notes.3ciii: The equation for the reaction was reasonably attempted on the whole. Most took the information offered by (i) and (ii) and gave equations with sodium hydroxide as the product along with hydrogen gas.
notes.3di: Galvanising was widely known as the name of the process in which iron is coated in zinc.
notes.3dii: Most candidates talked about sacrificial methods of rust protection rather than the obvious barrier to water / oxygen that a complete layer on the surface of the iron would afford.
notes.3diii: This question asked how zinc blocks (rather than a complete layer of zinc) prevented rusting. Many responses indicated an understanding of rusting that goes beyond the requirements of IGCSE. At this level it was sufficient to state that zinc is more reactive than iron and therefore will corrode in preference to iron. Directions of electron flow / exchange are not needed. Candidates need to be aware that zinc does not rust in preference to iron.
notes.4a: Although the correct answer, ‘hydrocarbons’, was very widely known other responses such as ‘carbohydrate’ or ‘hydrogen carbonate’ were fairly regularly seen.
notes.4bi: The idea that addition reactions are those which produce a single product was not widely known. Many candidates gave descriptions of addition polymerisation which, although one particular type of addition reaction, was far too narrow an answer.
notes.4bii: Most candidates were able to draw a chain of three single-bonded carbon atoms. Only the best responses placed bromine atoms on positions 1 and 2. Common incorrect structures were 1,1-dibromopropane, 1,3-dibromopropane and monobromopropane.
notes.4biii: The change in colour associated with the test for unsaturation was widely known.
notes.4biv: This demanding question proved difficult for many candidates. For those who understood that alkenes were required as the answer, the structure of but-2-ene was frequently seen, but usually accompanied by methylpropene. Many weaker responses had structures with trivalent or pentavalent carbon atoms and many included alcohols.
notes.4c: Many realised that HC l must be a product of this substitution reaction, but significantly fewer were able to construct the full equation.
notes.5ai: Many candidates omitted the one key condition, the presence of an acid (as a catalyst).
notes.5aii: Most candidates knew the type of chemical change from ethanol to ethanoic acid was an oxidation.
notes.5aiii: The ability to convert the structure of ethanoic acid into a dot-and-cross diagram was done well. Candidates should understand that a single bond is one dot/cross pair and double bonds are two dot/cross pairs. All the non-bonding electrons were frequently omitted.
notes.5b: Nearly every candidate knew that partial dissociation occurs in weak acids and full dissociation takes place in strong acids. ‘High dissociation’ was not credited. Most candidates realised that two ‘acidic’ colours were required and that the colour of the strong acid should be more acidic than that of the weak acid. Typical successful combinations were orange and red. Successful candidates gave effervescence as the observation and stated it was more vigorous with strong acids. Common errors were to say ‘little or no effervescence’ with a weak acid; failure to indicate the effervescence was greater with strong acids, or to say ‘slow reaction and fast reaction’ without including any observation. Cambridge International General Certificate of Secondary Education 0620 Chemistry November 2020
notes.5ci: The vast majority of candidates knew water was produced during ester formation.
notes.5cii: Many differing irrelevant sets of conditions were seen but as long as candidates knew an acid (as a catalyst) was needed, credit was given.
notes.5ciii: Candidates needed to identify that the 3-carbon alcohol was propan-2-ol, rather than the more commonly seen propan-1-ol. Some candidates realised an alcohol was needed, but many candidates incorrectly drew trivalent carbon atoms in their structures.
notes.5di: Candidates found it difficult to explain the meaning of the term functional group . Many related it to the identification of molecules or to homologous series.
notes.5dii: Empirical formula was not clearly understood with many giving the molecular formula as well as hybrid formulae such as C 2 H 4 COOH.
notes.5diii: Many responses contained errors. These included, incorrect M r values; not appreciating the total mass of oxygen present was 32; failure to give an answer to a whole number and inverted fractions yielding answers in excess of 100% were frequently seen.
notes.5div: Most candidates were able to draw an ester linkage showing all the bonds, but many could get no further due to either the incorrect orientation of ester links or the omission of continuation bonds.
notes.5dv: Many candidates were able to recall that Terylene was a polyester. Some candidates struggled to present an unambiguous spelling of Terylene . Cambridge International General Certificate of Secondary Education 0620 Chemistry November 2020
